readerTitle: The discount that filled the calendar and emptied the till
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소 서비스, B2B 회계·IT 관리 서비스) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 할인은 쓰는 모든 고객에게 돈을 내주지만, 수익은 할인 때문에 행동을 바꾼 고객에게서만 나온다. 할인은 '얼마나 깎나'보다 '누구에게, 무엇과 맞바꿔 주나'로 판단한다.
misconception: 할인으로 판매량이 늘었으면 할인이 성공한 것이다.

sources.text: 가격 전략의 표준 개념 (증분 판매와 '어차피 살 고객'에 대한 보조, 조건부 할인)

factChecks.note: 신규 고객 한정 $30 할인 시: 기존 200건 $12,000 그대로 + 신규 40건 × $30 = $1,200, 합계 $13,200. 신규 고객이 같은 40건 들어온다는 가정입니다.
청소 건당 비용 $60에는 인건비와 소모품만 포함하고 카드 수수료 등은 단순화를 위해 뺐습니다.

cards.title: The discount that filled the calendar and emptied the till
body: A home cleaning company had a slow January. The owner cut every price by 25%.
Bookings went up 20%. The team was busier than in any January before. And the month left 40% less money than doing nothing would have.

image.label: A packed booking calendar next to a nearly empty cash jar
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 칸이 빽빽하게 찬 월간 예약 달력, 오른쪽에 동전이 바닥에만 조금 남은 유리 저금통. 청소 도구(대걸레, 스프레이병)가 달력 옆에 기대어 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: January is slow. How do you discount?
body: You run a home cleaning service: about 200 cleans a month at $120, mostly regular clients. Each clean costs you about $60 in staff time and supplies.
You want more bookings this month. Which discount do you pick?

options.text: 25% off every clean in January, for everyone
options.feedback: It's simple and draws new clients. But your 200 regulars would have booked anyway, and each of them now pays $30 less.

options.text: $30 off the first clean, for new clients only
options.feedback: The money goes only to people who weren't booking before. Your regulars keep paying full price, so every new job is pure gain.

options.text: 25% off weekday-morning slots, your quietest times, for everyone
options.feedback: It fills idle hours, which is smart. But many regulars will simply move their usual clean into the cheaper slot.

cards.title: Where the money went with 25% off for everyone.
body: Before: 200 cleans leaving $60 each, or **$12,000**. After: 240 cleans leaving $30 each, or $7,200. The 40 new jobs were real. They just cost far less than the gift to everyone else.

breakdown.label: Regular clients
breakdown.detail: 200 cleans that would have happened anyway × $30 less

breakdown.label: Net result
breakdown.detail: A busier month that earned 40% less

cards.title: A discount pays everyone, but earns only from some.
body: **Discounting** means selling below your normal price to win a sale. Every customer who uses the discount gets the money. But you only gain from the ones it actually changes: people who buy now, buy more, or buy at all because of it.
Sales you would have made anyway are not wins. They're **giveaways**. A good discount is aimed so that as little of it as possible lands on those customers.

image.label: A funnel of discount coins, most falling on customers who were already buying
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 위에서 할인 동전이 쏟아지고, 아래에 사람 두 그룹. 큰 그룹 "Would have bought anyway"에 동전 대부분이 떨어지고, 작은 그룹 "Changed by the discount"에만 초록 체크 표시. 단순한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: Three ways to aim a discount.
body: Before offering money off, decide who should get it and what you get back.
list: **Fence it:** only new customers, only first orders, only idle times that regulars can't easily switch into
**Trade it:** give a lower price in exchange for something you value, like a longer commitment, payment upfront or flexible scheduling
**Cap it:** limit it by date or quantity so it can't quietly become the new normal price
cards.callout: Ask of every discount: who gets this who would have paid full price?
cards.softwareNote: Software companies often trade a discount for commitment: about two months free on an annual plan paid upfront. The customer saves money, and the company gets cash now and fewer cancellations.

cards.title: Fences have costs too.
body: Loyal clients can feel cheated when strangers get a better deal. A new-client-only offer may need a small thank-you for regulars, or it can cost you trust.
Fences also leak. Regulars can sign up under a partner's name, and conditions that feel like hoops can put off the very people you wanted.
And a discount only helps if you can serve the extra work. If it means turning away full-price jobs, the gain shrinks fast.

cards.title: Now a client asks you for 15% off.
body: Your firm provides outsourced bookkeeping and IT support. A business client pays $4,000 a month and its one-year contract is up for renewal. Their manager asks for 15% off, which would cost you $7,200 a year.

options.text: Agree to 15% off to keep a good client
options.feedback: You probably keep them, but you give away $7,200 for nothing in return, and you teach them that asking works every year.

options.text: Hold the price and remind them of the value you deliver
options.feedback: This protects your price and may work if they're happy. If they have a real alternative, you risk losing $48,000 a year to save $7,200.

options.text: Offer 8% off if they sign for two years and pay quarterly upfront
options.feedback: You give up $3,840 a year but get a longer commitment and earlier cash. The discount buys you something instead of leaking away.

cards.title: Discount for the sales you'd lose, not the ones you'd get anyway.
body: More sales doesn't mean the discount worked. Count what it cost on the customers who would have paid full price.
**Try it today:** look at your last discount. Estimate how many buyers would have bought anyway, and what you gave them in total.
